title: The Golden Gate Bridge
subtitle: What has stood across the mouth of San Francisco Bay since 1937, and what it has taken to keep it there.
description: A B1 reading and listening text on the Golden Gate Bridge — its construction, its color, its fog and its maintenance — written to practice the present perfect, with vocabulary and comprehension exercises.
passage: The Golden Gate Bridge has stood across the entrance to San Francisco Bay since 1937, and in that time it has become one of the most recognizable structures in the world. It was a genuinely difficult thing to build. The strait it crosses is deep, the current runs hard through it twice a day, and the fog can close in within minutes. Plenty of engineers said at the time that a bridge there could not be built at all.

It was built anyway, as a suspension bridge, with a main span of about 1,280 meters. That made it the longest suspension span in the world when it opened, and it held that record for twenty-seven years. The two towers rise 227 meters above the water, and for a long time they were the tallest things in the city by a wide margin.

The color was an accident that stuck. The steel arrived coated in a reddish primer, and the consulting architect argued that the color suited the setting better than the gray or the black-and-yellow stripes that had been proposed. The shade is called International Orange, and it has turned out to have a practical advantage as well: it stays visible in fog, which matters on a strait where the fog is a daily fact for much of the summer.

Building it cost lives, though fewer than expected. A safety net was strung beneath the deck — an unusual precaution at the time, and an expensive one — and it caught nineteen men who would otherwise have fallen to their deaths. They called themselves the Halfway to Hell Club. Eleven workers died on the project, ten of them in a single accident near the end when a section of scaffolding fell through the net.

Since it opened, more than two billion vehicles have crossed the bridge. It has survived earthquakes, including the one in 1989 that brought down part of another bridge in the same bay, and it has since been strengthened further against the next one. It has been closed to traffic only a handful of times, almost always because of wind.

Keeping it standing is constant work. Crews have been maintaining and repainting the bridge continuously since it opened; the popular belief that they finish one end and immediately start again at the other is not quite accurate, but the ironworkers and painters have never really stopped. Salt air attacks steel, and a structure this size in this position would not last a decade without them.

What has not changed is what people do when they get there. They stop, they look, and they take a photograph in more or less the same spot, whether they have driven across it every working day for thirty years or have arrived from the other side of the world to see it once.

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: Answer from the meaning of the text.

items.prompt: Why did engineers say a bridge could not be built there?
options: Because the strait is deep, the current is strong and the fog closes in quickly
Because there was no demand for a crossing
Because the city could not afford it
items.explanation: All three conditions are given, and the paragraph ends with the claim that it “could not be built at all”.

items.prompt: How long did the bridge hold the record for the longest suspension span?
items.explanation: It opened in 1937 with the longest span in the world “and it held that record for twenty-seven years”.

items.prompt: How was the bridge's colour chosen?
options: It was selected to match the surrounding hills
It was required by aviation regulations
The steel arrived in a reddish primer and the architect argued for keeping that colour
items.explanation: “The colour was an accident that stuck” — grey and black-and-yellow stripes had been proposed instead.

items.prompt: What practical advantage does International Orange turn out to have?
options: It resists salt corrosion better than other colours
It fades more slowly in sunlight
items.explanation: Which matters because the fog is “a daily fact for much of the summer”.

items.prompt: What was the Halfway to Hell Club?
options: The engineers who insisted the bridge was possible
The crew who worked the night shift
The nineteen men the safety net caught before they hit the water
items.explanation: They named themselves after surviving a fall that would otherwise have killed them.

items.prompt: Why does the text say the bridge would not last a decade without maintenance?
options: Because the traffic load is too heavy
Because the towers are slowly sinking
items.explanation: “Salt air attacks steel, and a structure this size in this position would not last a decade without them.”

items.prompt: How does the writer correct the popular belief about repainting?
options: By saying the bridge has never been repainted
By saying the belief is not quite accurate, though the work has never really stopped
By saying the painting is now done once every ten years
items.explanation: The writer neither repeats the myth nor dismisses the underlying truth — continuous maintenance is real, the end-to-end story is not.

items.prompt: What point is the final paragraph making?
options: That the bridge is too crowded with tourists
That daily commuters and first-time visitors react to it in the same way
items.explanation: “Whether they have driven across it every working day for thirty years or have arrived from the other side of the world to see it once.”

exercises.title: Present Perfect or Past Simple?
exercises.instructions: Use the past simple for a finished action at a stated past time, and the present perfect for something that runs from the past up to now, or whose time is not stated.

items.prompt: The bridge ___ across the bay since 1937.
items.explanation: “Since” marks a period running up to now, which always takes the present perfect.

items.prompt: It ___ in 1937, after four years of construction.
items.explanation: A finished event at a stated past time takes the past simple. Compare the sentence above.

items.prompt: More than two billion vehicles ___ the bridge since it opened.
items.explanation: A total accumulating from the past up to the present moment.

items.prompt: The safety net ___ nineteen men during construction.
items.explanation: The construction period is over, so the past simple. The net is no longer catching anyone.

items.prompt: Crews ___ the bridge continuously since it opened.
items.explanation: Present perfect continuous: an activity that started in the past, has continued, and is still going on.

items.prompt: It ___ several earthquakes, and it ___ further after the one in 1989.
items.explanation: The first has no stated time and continues to be true; the second is tied to a specific year, so past simple passive.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the text.

items.statement: The bridge is still the longest suspension span in the world.
items.explanation: False — it held that record for twenty-seven years after opening.

items.statement: The orange colour was chosen before the steel arrived.
items.explanation: False — the steel arrived in a reddish primer, and the architect argued for keeping it.

items.statement: The safety net saved more workers than the number who died.
items.explanation: True — nineteen were caught by the net; eleven died.

items.statement: Most of the deaths happened in one accident.
items.explanation: True — ten of the eleven, when scaffolding fell through the net near the end of the work.

items.statement: The bridge closes to traffic frequently.
items.explanation: False — “only a handful of times, almost always because of wind”.

discussion: Engineers said the bridge could not be built. What makes people attempt something after being told that?
The safety net was unusual and expensive, and it saved nineteen lives. How should that cost be weighed when it is being decided?
The color was an accident that turned out to work. Can you think of something in your own life that worked out the same way?
Is there a structure in your country that people photograph in the same spot every time? Why that one?
Write about 120 words describing a famous structure you have seen, using the present perfect for what it has done and the past simple for when it was built.
